comment: “Hello council members, Both in June and July I wrote in to digitally participate in the online only council meeting. I submitted questions and concerns and requests similar to other residents who did the same. I have not received a response yet so I am sending in the requests below to be addressed in the council meeting. If comments from the public are not addressed in the meeting itself, I would ask for a response via email. With the process of hiring a new police chief, there is a lot to be considered and a lot of input the public would like to weigh in on. I would like to request the council to start the process of organizing such a civilian/citizen oversight board that can not only in the future help with internal reviews, but can also be a part of the hiring process of the new chief. In addition to the immediate need of a developed citizen review board, I'd like to request the council review and address solutions for the below as soon as possible. Chief Giles went over some of these and mentioned that some of these are state laws but there seemed to be quite a lot of room for exceptions. My request would be that we locally explicitly unauthorize many of these things WITHOUT exceptions: Use of Force A. Authorize deadly force only when there is an imminent threat to an officer's life or the life of another person and such force is strictly unavoidable to protect life as required under International Law. Require officers give a verbal warning, when possible, before using deadly force and give people a reasonable amount of time to comply with the warning. Chief Giles mentioned this is also a state law but there are exceptions. Can we eliminate exceptions locally? D. Require reporting of police killings and serious injuries of civilians E. Require the names of both the officer(s) involved and victim(s) to be released within 72 hours of a deadly force incident. Revise and strengthen local police department use of force policies. Revised police use of force policies should protect human life and rights. Policies should include guidance on reporting, investigation, discipline, and accountability and increase transparency by making the policies available online. comment: “We are compelled to make yet another appeal to preserve the Lakeview community. But first, let’s express gratitude where it is due: We applaud the City Council that presided over the Southwest Annexation with their rejection of high density development on the parcel that is now Wilkerson Farms. We are grateful to the many who voiced their opposition to the urbanization of Lakeview. We are grateful to the Orem City Council members who listened to the public and voted accordingly. We are grateful for the miracle that ensued as the Wilkerson family refused to give up on their dream. They worked doggedly to protect agriculture and open space. Even I, who hoped desperately for their success, thought they would fail. Much to the shock of everyone, including developers and the Orem City Council, the Wilkerson family scored an upset victory for the ages. We can’t thank them enough for their persistence, courage, and grit against all odds. Is there a citizen in Orem who can drive by Wilkerson Farms without a spark of joy and pride that it is part of our city? So where is all of the vocal opposition that enabled the preservation of Wilkerson Farms? Some were farmers who leased and were forced off the land by development. Others have been worn down over time by meeting after meeting that almost always favors developers. It has become apparent that city officials and developers have formed a de facto alliance. The voices of those who seek to preserve a shred of Lakeview’s historical appeal as a community have been silenced. To that point, please consider the following: • In one city council meeting I made a suggestion to consider residential development west of our farm instead of light industrial development. In no uncertain terms I was instructed that even if the zoning were changed the resulting increase in population was impossible to consider due to the sizing of the sewer line. Some months later we learned that Orem City was pushing to increase residential density in the Lakeview area. Wait—what about the undersized sewer? Not a problem. It appears that Orem City has different answers to the same question. It just depends on who’s asking the question. • In another meeting developers submitted a plan that exceeded density as defined by the zoning. Appropriately, the city council denied the request. However, in that same meeting, in front of all of us who opposed the higher density, they schooled the developers on how they could work to achieve their desired density with a PD zone. Now that the city wants to increase density by revising the city plan, developers will have clear sailing without the bother of a PD zone. • It now appears that the compromised density balance achieved at the time of annexation was a sham. A classic bait and switch. The city is now looking at the planned temple as a vehicle to increase density though it remains a mystery as to the logical connection. More reasoned thinking suggests that increased traffic resulting from the temple should be balanced by lower density in surrounding neighborhoods, not higher. • The city’s use of virtual meetings has throttled the voice of Orem citizens. I learned after the July 15th Planning Commission meeting of those who are technology savvy yet failed to connect to the meeting. I understood their complaints. I personally had difficulty getting into the meeting. The instructions were not clear and the hyperlinks were not obvious. I tried several PC browsers as well as my cell phone before I succeeded in joining the meeting. • Instead of the critical and appropriately emotional discourse that is vital to such community meetings, virtual meetings deliver a sterile communication vacuum that stifles meaningful discourse, especially since they are designed for pushing out information by those who control the technology. They are poorly designed for receiving feedback from the public. Moreover, I suspect it is much easier for Planning Commission and City Council members to ignore our arguments when they don’t have to look us in the eye. • A review of Southwest Annexation records reveals the volume and intensity of opposition to higher density in Lakeview. While the opportunity for expression is now suppressed, the risks and problems articulated in 2015 persist. In fact they’re getting worse. • Most of my comments provided to the July 15th Planning Commission meeting were ignored. However, for the first time it was tacitly acknowledged by an Orem City official that traffic on Geneva Road is only going to get worse as density increases, and that farming will be increasingly difficult. Regrettably, the topic was dismissed with a virtual shrug of the shoulders. comment: To Richard Brunst, Orem City Mayor It is with deep concern that I am writing regarding the proposal of increased density along Geneva Road in the Lakeview area. It is a recognized fact that farming and agricultural pursuits have been the foundation and strength for generations in this area. Over time, and at present, developers have seen these fields and farmlands as a prime location. It was through compromise, while tough, of those who valued open space and continued to work the land, and those whose desire it was to develop the properties, that annexation by Orem City was realized several years ago. Affordable housing is a matter which is readily addressed by those wishing to develop and construct living space. The Fields at Lakeview located at 1884 South on Geneva Road, presently being the homes of many, and with ample construction continuing, is a clear and adequate response to this. I find it most difficult to comprehend the request for a change to allow increased housing density. Just less than a year ago, September 2019, the City Council voted against increasing the density. I now ask why the thrust for rezoning that would allow for even greater density? The welcoming atmosphere of neighborhoods without crowded housing is to be valued by all. Additionally, do not ignore the rise of traffic on Geneva Road. This will come with increased density. As landowners we will continue to farm our land. The inevitable growth of traffic that would accompany the zoning change will definitely be a significant difficulty with both traffic and farming. It is imperative that you, Mayor Brunst, as mayor of Orem City, listen to, and recognize, and accept the voice of we who value open space, who live here, and who will continue farming the land. I urge you to refrain from any changes that will increase the density in the Lakeview area of Geneva Road.

comment: The following is a summary of the housing in the Lake View Area from University Parkway south to 2000 South and from I-15 West: Name of Development Number of Units Percentage Rentals Village on the Parkway 72 100% (single student housing 4 to 5 students/apartment) Oakhurst 128 100% (128 units) Country Woods 180 66% (119 units) Normandy 52 69% (36 units) Chambery 160 65% (104 units) Fields (Jeff Mansell) 78* 55 % (43 units) *This number changes frequently In summary, eliminating Village on the Parkway which was built as student housing, there are 598 units consisting of apartments, townhomes and condos with 72 % (430 units) being rentals. We have only 21 individual homes in the area. There are currently 7 individual homes being built in Payton’s Crossing. There are no individual homes planned in the Fields. With the exception of Oakhurst and Village on the Parkway, all of these developments were presented in the planning process as owner occupied. We have more than enough rentals in the area. We have a drastic shortage of individual homes. We want homes where families will come, raise their families, and stay for the rest of their lives. We are requesting that the residential areas in the Lake View area be zoned at 4 units/acre with no option for an increase in density. This will provide more stability and allow the neighborhood to develop with character similar to the rest of Orem.
